title: Acid and Base Models: Arrhenius to Brønsted-Lowry | Year 12 Chemistry
description:

Ammonia turns litmus blue, but it has no hydroxide. Follow how the definition of an acid changed: Lavoisier's oxygen, Davy's hydrogen, Arrhenius's ions in water, and Brønsted-Lowry proton transfer. description:

Did penicillin make bacteria resistant, or was resistance already there? title: Weak Acid and Weak Base pH with ICE Tables, Ka and Kb | Year 12 Chemistry
description:
Full lesson, notes and practice questions: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12/module6/lesson09.sa.html

Treat propanoic acid like hydrochloric acid and you predict pH 0.824; the pH meter reads 2.85. See why: a weak acid stays mostly un-ionised, so its hydronium concentration is far below its concentration. Then use Ka and an ICE table step by step: set up the table, drop x when Ka is tiny, check that x is under 5%, find the equilibrium concentrations and the pH. NESA's marking feedback flags the same problem every year: answers that respond to a slightly different question from the one asked. Learn a four-step reading routine for every exam question: the verb (do what?), the marks (how much?), the content words and givens (about what?), and the constraint (using what?). See what "in terms of", "with reference to" and "using the information" really ask for, and why "one mark, one idea" is only a rule of thumb. Then try two HSC-style training questions, one in Chemistry and one in Biology. All questions are written for HSCScience in the HSC style; they are not official NESA questions.

description:
Year 12 Chemistry: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/chemistry/year12
Year 12 Biology: https://hscscience.com.au/subjects/biology/year12

"Explain" is the most common key word in recent HSC Chemistry and Biology written sections: 57 question parts in the 2021 to 2025 papers, usually for 2 to 4 marks. Learn what identify, describe and explain each ask you to write, using one HSC-style genetics question answered at all three levels. See why explain means showing how one thing causes the next, why a "because" on its own is not enough, and how a description posing as an explanation loses marks. Then try two training questions, one in Chemistry and one in Biology. All questions are written for HSCScience in the HSC style; they are not official NESA questions.
